message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for highly parallel tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each core is powerful, with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of lightweight cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core is simpler but many can work simultaneously on the same instruction stream. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex, rich set of instructions, supports branching, recursion, and varied data types. | Often a reduced instruction set optimized for throughput; less emphasis on branching. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory interface, low latency access. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). Latency is higher, but bandwidth is massive. |
| **Workload Suitability** | Serial or lightly parallel tasks, heavy branching, unpredictable memory accesses. | Data‑parallel tasks where the same operation is applied to many independent data elements (e.g., matrix multiplication, image filtering). |
| **Typical Use Cases** | Running operating systems, web browsers, office software, database engines, general programming. | Rendering 3D graphics, video encoding/decoding, scientific simulations, deep learning inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power & Heat** | Designed for efficiency at lower clock speeds; thermal limits are tighter for single cores. | Can run at very high core counts; GPUs often have dedicated cooling solutions and can consume more power overall. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, sequential tasks quickly with low latency, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on a huge amount of data simultaneously, trading off per‑core performance for sheer parallel throughput.
